views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay inside the G20 90-day window and treat the just-concluded Beijing working talks as the start of a deal path, not a moment to escalate or to surrender industrial policy. Offer substantial, verifiable purchases of US farm, energy and some manufactured goods as the main concession, while refusing one-sided structural commitments and enforcement mechanisms that would gut Made in China 2025. Do not add new tariffs or further hostage diplomacy; the March 2 List-3 cliff and a possible List-4 covering remaining exports would hit an already slowing economy harder than another round of Chinese retaliation would hurt the United States.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. US Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese goods (25% on the $50B Lists 1–2; 10% on List 3), with the List-3 rate scheduled to jump to 25% if there is no deal by ~2 March 2019 (timeline 2018-09-17/24; 2018-12-01 truce only suspended that hike). That is a major export-sector hit, and the non-tariff track is worse for national champions: the April 2018 ZTE denial order showed Washington can shut a firm down, and the 1 December arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou on a US extradition request, plus Beijing’s subsequent detention of two Canadians, has fused the trade fight to tech self-sufficiency and political legitimacy. Macro corroboration is one-sided in the official health file (CHN series empty) but contemporaneous reporting is consistent: Q3 2018 GDP slowed to 6.5%, the weakest since 2009; World Bank (Dec 2018) had equities −20% and the RMB −6% vs USD, with 2019 growth marked down to 6.2%; PBOC had already cut RRR four times in 2018. US customs imports from China in the health file fell from $52.1B (Oct) to $41.3B (Jan), a ~14% drop over the window — consistent with tariff diversion and front-loading fading. This sits near the CHN +0.5 anchor (major export sectors hit, FX pressure, Huawei-style firm targeting) but short of +1.0: growth is still officially in the mid-6s, the January hike was postponed, and talks are live.

Action should be negotiate, not escalate or concede. Jan 7–9 Beijing talks were extended a third day; Trump called them “going very well,” and reporting shows progress on purchases, GM-crop approvals and market access, but a clear gap on IP/tech-transfer and how Beijing would be held to promises (CNBC/Guardian 9 Jan 2019). China Daily already set the red line: no “unreasonable concessions.” Escalating tariffs or further non-tariff moves now would likely bring the 25% List-3 hike forward and invite the threatened ~$267B List 4, which China cannot match dollar-for-dollar. Unilateral rollback or locked-in structural reform would trade away the industrial-policy core before the US has offered a matching tariff cut. Purchases are the right bargaining chip — China already made large soybean buys and issued GM approvals as goodwill — but they should be packaged inside talks, not prepaid. Second-order: US farm-belt pain and a January drop in US consumer sentiment to 91.2 give Washington some incentive to deal; use that, do not assume it.
key_factors: List 3 10%→25% cliff around 2 March 2019 still hanging over ~$200B of exports
Huawei/Meng arrest plus earlier ZTE denial order = firm-level tech threat, not just tariffs
Domestic slowdown (Q3 GDP 6.5%, RMB/equities down, RRR cuts) raises cost of further escalation
Beijing talks show purchase/market-access progress but no deal on structural IP/industrial policy
Asymmetric retaliation capacity: US can still cover remaining ~$267B; China already used most of its US-goods tariff space

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 dinner: 90-day window; planned Jan 1 List-3 hike to 25% suspended at 10%. Same day Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou on a US extradition request.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China retaliates 5–10% on ~$60B. Combined US Section 301 coverage ~$250B.
Trade talks resume in Beijing (working/mid-level). China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
US Commerce bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). Major non-tariff escalation.
US imports from China fell from $52.1B (2018-10) to $41.3B (2019-01), about -14% over the window.
US Michigan sentiment dropped to 91.2 in January 2019 from 98.3 in December.

Talks extended to a third day; progress on farm/energy purchases and market access; sides further apart on structural reforms and enforcement. No deal by March 2 → 25% on $200B. China Daily: no unreasonable concessions.
Q3 GDP 6.5%; equities -20%; RMB -6% vs USD; World Bank projected 6.5% in 2018 and 6.2% in 2019.
